title: CHAPTER I. Mrs. Rachel Lynde Is Surprised

source.notice: 原文来自 Project Gutenberg，保留原书来源及许可；各地区版权规则可能不同。

paragraphs.en: MRS. Rachel Lynde lived just where the Avonlea main road dipped down into a little hollow, fringed with alders and ladies’ eardrops and traversed by a brook that had its source away back in the woods of the old Cuthbert place; it was reputed to be an intricate, headlong brook in its earlier course through those woods, with dark secrets of pool and cascade; but by the time it reached Lynde’s Hollow it was a quiet, well-conducted little stream, for not even a brook could run past Mrs. Rachel Lynde’s door without due regard for decency and decorum; it probably was conscious that Mrs. Rachel was sitting at her window, keeping a sharp eye on everything that passed, from brooks and children up, and that if she noticed anything odd or out of place she would never rest until she had ferreted out the whys and wherefores thereof.
paragraphs.zh: 拉塞尔夫人住在阿文利亚主路低洼处的一所房子里，那里被桤木和耳叶悬钩子所环绕，一条小溪从那里流过，这条小溪的源头远在库瑟伯特家旧林地的深处；据说这条小溪在穿过那片树林时，是一条曲折湍急的溪流，隐藏着许多深不可测的水潭和瀑布；但等到它流到莱恩德洼地时，却变成了一条安静、规矩的小溪，因为就连一条小溪也不可能在经过拉塞尔夫人门前时，不注意体面和规矩；它也许意识到了拉塞尔夫人 坐在窗边，她仔细地注视着一切经过的事物，从小溪和孩子们一直到其他一切，如果她发现有什么异常或不寻常的地方，她绝不会安心，直到她弄清楚其中的原委。

paragraphs.en: There are plenty of people, in Avonlea and out of it, who can attend closely to their neighbors’ business by dint of neglecting their own; but Mrs. Rachel Lynde was one of those capable creatures who can manage their own concerns and those of other folks into the bargain. She was a notable housewife; her work was always done and well done; she “ran” the Sewing Circle, helped run the Sunday-school, and was the strongest prop of the Church Aid Society and Foreign Missions Auxiliary. Yet with all this Mrs. Rachel found abundant time to sit for hours at her kitchen window, knitting “cotton warp” quilts--she had knitted sixteen of them, as Avonlea housekeepers were wont to tell in awed voices--and keeping a sharp eye on the main road that crossed the hollow and wound up the steep red hill beyond. Since Avonlea occupied a little triangular peninsula jutting out into the Gulf of St. Lawrence, with water on two sides of it, anybody who went out of it or into it had to pass over that hill road and so run the unseen gauntlet of Mrs. Rachel’s all-seeing eye.
paragraphs.zh: 在阿文利和外面，有许多人能够密切关注邻居的事务，却疏于料理自己的事；但瑞秋·莱德夫人却是个能干的人，她不仅能料理好自己的事，还能帮别人把事情也料理得妥妥当当。她是个出色的管家，她的活儿总是做得又快又好；她主持“缝纫会”，协助管理主日学，还是“教会援助协会”和“海外传教辅助会”的中坚力量。然而，尽管有这么多事务要处理，瑞秋·莱德夫人仍有充足的时间坐在厨房的窗边，一坐就是好几个小时，织着“棉线经纱”。 被褥——她织了十六条，正如阿文利的主妇们用敬畏的语气讲述的那样——并且时刻留意着穿过山谷、蜿蜒爬上那座陡峭的红山的主要道路。由于阿文利位于一个伸入圣劳伦斯湾的小三角半岛上，它三面环水，因此任何进出阿文利的人都必须经过那条山路，从而不可避免地经过蕾切尔夫人那双无所不见的眼睛的监视。

paragraphs.en: She was sitting there one afternoon in early June. The sun was coming in at the window warm and bright; the orchard on the slope below the house was in a bridal flush of pinky-white bloom, hummed over by a myriad of bees. Thomas Lynde--a meek little man whom Avonlea people called “Rachel Lynde’s husband”--was sowing his late turnip seed on the hill field beyond the barn; and Matthew Cuthbert ought to have been sowing his on the big red brook field away over by Green Gables. Mrs. Rachel knew that he ought because she had heard him tell Peter Morrison the evening before in William J. Blair’s store over at Carmody that he meant to sow his turnip seed the next afternoon. Peter had asked him, of course, for Matthew Cuthbert had never been known to volunteer information about anything in his whole life.
paragraphs.zh: 有一天下午，她坐在那里，那是六月的早些时候。阳光从窗户照进来，温暖而明亮；房子下方山坡上的果园里，桃李花盛开，呈现出新娘般的粉白色，成群的蜜蜂在花间嗡嗡飞舞。托马斯·林德——一个性格温顺的小个子男人，阿文利的居民都称他为“瑞秋·林德的丈夫”——正在谷仓外的山坡地上播种晚熟的萝卜种子；而马修·卡思伯特本应该在绿屋农场那边的大红溪地里播种他的萝卜种子。瑞秋夫人知道他应该在那里播种，因为她前一天晚上听到他跟彼得·莫里森在威廉·J·布雷尔家说过。 他把这事告诉了卡莫迪家，说他打算第二天下午种他的萝卜种子。当然，彼得问他了，因为马修·卡瑟伯从来不会主动提供任何信息。

paragraphs.en: And yet here was Matthew Cuthbert, at half-past three on the afternoon of a busy day, placidly driving over the hollow and up the hill; moreover, he wore a white collar and his best suit of clothes, which was plain proof that he was going out of Avonlea; and he had the buggy and the sorrel mare, which betokened that he was going a considerable distance. Now, where was Matthew Cuthbert going and why was he going there?
paragraphs.zh: 然而，马修·卡瑟伯特此刻却出现在这里：在忙碌的一天下午三点过三分，他平静地驱车驶过低洼地带，爬上山丘；而且，他戴着白领子，穿着他最好的一套衣服，这明显说明他要离开阿文利了；他还套上了马车和那匹栗色母马，这说明他要前往相当远的地方。那么，马修·卡瑟伯特要去哪里，又为什么要去那里呢？

paragraphs.en: Had it been any other man in Avonlea, Mrs. Rachel, deftly putting this and that together, might have given a pretty good guess as to both questions. But Matthew so rarely went from home that it must be something pressing and unusual which was taking him; he was the shyest man alive and hated to have to go among strangers or to any place where he might have to talk. Matthew, dressed up with a white collar and driving in a buggy, was something that didn’t happen often. Mrs. Rachel, ponder as she might, could make nothing of it and her afternoon’s enjoyment was spoiled.
paragraphs.zh: 如果是阿文利亚的其他任何人，蕾切尔太太机灵地把这和那联系起来，也许就能对这两个问题做出相当准确的猜测。但马修很少离开家，所以一定是有什么紧急而不同寻常的事情在等着他；他是世上最腼腆的人，讨厌不得不去见陌生人，或者任何可能需要他说话的地方。马修穿着整洁，戴着白领子，坐着马车外出，这可不是常有的事。蕾切尔太太怎么也想不明白，她整个下午的兴致都被破坏了。

paragraphs.en: “I’ll just step over to Green Gables after tea and find out from Marilla where he’s gone and why,” the worthy woman finally concluded. “He doesn’t generally go to town this time of year and he _never_ visits; if he’d run out of turnip seed he wouldn’t dress up and take the buggy to go for more; he wasn’t driving fast enough to be going for a doctor. Yet something must have happened since last night to start him off. I’m clean puzzled, that’s what, and I won’t know a minute’s peace of mind or conscience until I know what has taken Matthew Cuthbert out of Avonlea today.”
paragraphs.zh: “我吃完茶后就去绿屋看看，从玛丽拉那儿弄清楚他去哪儿了，为什么去，”这位正派的妇人最后说道。“他这个季节一般不会去镇上，而且他从不外出；如果他把芜菁种子用完了，也不会穿上衣服，坐马车去再买一些；他开车又不够快，不可能是去请医生。但昨晚以来一定发生了什么事，才让他今天离开阿文利。我真是想不通，我就是弄不明白，直到我知道马修·卡瑟伯特今天为什么离开了阿文利，我一刻也得不到安宁和心安。”

paragraphs.en: Accordingly after tea Mrs. Rachel set out; she had not far to go; the big, rambling, orchard-embowered house where the Cuthberts lived was a scant quarter of a mile up the road from Lynde’s Hollow. To be sure, the long lane made it a good deal further. Matthew Cuthbert’s father, as shy and silent as his son after him, had got as far away as he possibly could from his fellow men without actually retreating into the woods when he founded his homestead. Green Gables was built at the furthest edge of his cleared land and there it was to this day, barely visible from the main road along which all the other Avonlea houses were so sociably situated. Mrs. Rachel Lynde did not call living in such a place _living_ at all.
paragraphs.zh: 因此，茶后，拉塞尔夫人出发了；她不需要走很远；库瑟伯特家那座大而杂乱、被果园环绕的房子，就在林德小屋上方道路不到一英里处。当然，那条长长的车道使实际距离远得多。马修·库瑟伯特的父亲，和他后来的儿子一样害羞而沉默，当他建立自己的农庄时，尽可能远离他人，却又没有真正退居森林深处。绿屋就建在他开垦土地的最远处，直到今天，它仍从主路上几乎看不见。 其他阿文利的房子都住得这么热闹。拉塞尔·莱恩德夫人认为住在这样的地方根本不算“生活”。

paragraphs.en: “It’s just _staying_, that’s what,” she said as she stepped along the deep-rutted, grassy lane bordered with wild rose bushes. “It’s no wonder Matthew and Marilla are both a little odd, living away back here by themselves. Trees aren’t much company, though dear knows if they were there’d be enough of them. I’d ruther look at people. To be sure, they seem contented enough; but then, I suppose, they’re used to it. A body can get used to anything, even to being hanged, as the Irishman said.”
paragraphs.zh: “问题就在于‘待着’，就是这样，”她沿着布满车辙、长满青草、两旁长满野蔷薇灌木的小路走着说，“难怪马修和玛丽拉都多少有点怪，独自住在这偏僻的地方。树嘛，也谈不上是什么好伴儿，不过，天知道，如果有的话，肯定够多了。我宁愿看人。他们看起来倒是挺满足的；不过，我想他们已经习惯了。一个人什么事都能习惯，就连被绞死都能习惯，就像那个爱尔兰人说的。”

paragraphs.en: With this Mrs. Rachel stepped out of the lane into the backyard of Green Gables. Very green and neat and precise was that yard, set about on one side with great patriarchal willows and on the other with prim Lombardies. Not a stray stick nor stone was to be seen, for Mrs. Rachel would have seen it if there had been. Privately she was of the opinion that Marilla Cuthbert swept that yard over as often as she swept her house. One could have eaten a meal off the ground without overbrimming the proverbial peck of dirt.
paragraphs.zh: 这时，瑞秋太太走出了小巷，来到了绿屋的后院。这个院子非常翠绿、整洁而井然有序，一边种着高大庄严的柳树，另一边则是整齐划一的意大利杨树。院子里没有一根杂乱的树枝或一块石头，因为如果有的话，瑞秋太太一定会看到的。她私下认为，玛丽拉·卡斯伯特打扫院子的次数，和打扫她家房子的次数一样频繁。地面上干净得甚至可以在上面吃顿饭，而不会弄脏那 proverbial（谚语中）一蒲式耳的泥土。

paragraphs.en: Mrs. Rachel rapped smartly at the kitchen door and stepped in when bidden to do so. The kitchen at Green Gables was a cheerful apartment--or would have been cheerful if it had not been so painfully clean as to give it something of the appearance of an unused parlor. Its windows looked east and west; through the west one, looking out on the back yard, came a flood of mellow June sunlight; but the east one, whence you got a glimpse of the bloom white cherry-trees in the left orchard and nodding, slender birches down in the hollow by the brook, was greened over by a tangle of vines. Here sat Marilla Cuthbert, when she sat at all, always slightly distrustful of sunshine, which seemed to her too dancing and irresponsible a thing for a world which was meant to be taken seriously; and here she sat now, knitting, and the table behind her was laid for supper.
paragraphs.zh: 拉塞尔夫人在厨房门上敲了敲，随即在得到允许后走了进去。绿屋的厨房是个令人愉快的房间——如果它不是那么干净得过分，看起来像一间从未用过的客厅的话，那它本来会是令人愉快的。厨房的窗户朝东和西，西边的窗户朝向后院，洒进一片温暖的六月阳光；而东边的窗户则可以看到左边果园里盛开的白樱桃树，以及小溪边低洼处点头摇曳的纤细白桦树，但那扇窗户却被一片杂乱的藤蔓遮住了。她就坐在这里。 卡瑟琳夫人一坐下，总是对阳光抱有一丝怀疑，因为在她看来，阳光太活泼、太不负责任了，不适合一个应该认真对待的世界；此刻她正坐在那里织毛衣，她身后的桌子上已经摆好了晚餐。

paragraphs.en: Mrs. Rachel, before she had fairly closed the door, had taken a mental note of everything that was on that table. There were three plates laid, so that Marilla must be expecting some one home with Matthew to tea; but the dishes were everyday dishes and there was only crab-apple preserves and one kind of cake, so that the expected company could not be any particular company. Yet what of Matthew’s white collar and the sorrel mare? Mrs. Rachel was getting fairly dizzy with this unusual mystery about quiet, unmysterious Green Gables.
paragraphs.zh: 在蕾切尔夫人还没完全把门关上之前，她已经把桌上的一切都记在心里了。桌上有三个盘子，看来玛丽拉一定是在等有人和马修一起回来吃茶点；但盘子都是日常用的，只有苹果酱和一种蛋糕，所以被邀请来的客人应该不是什么特别的人物。然而马修的白领子和栗色母马又怎么解释呢？蕾切尔夫人对这个关于安静、毫无神秘感的绿山墙的不寻常谜团感到有些晕头转向了。

paragraphs.en: “Good evening, Rachel,” Marilla said briskly. “This is a real fine evening, isn’t it? Won’t you sit down? How are all your folks?”
paragraphs.zh: “晚上好，瑞秋，”玛丽拉干脆地说，“这是一个真正的美好夜晚，对吧？请坐吧。你家人都好吗？”

paragraphs.en: Something that for lack of any other name might be called friendship existed and always had existed between Marilla Cuthbert and Mrs. Rachel, in spite of--or perhaps because of--their dissimilarity.
paragraphs.zh: 在马莉拉·卡斯伯特和拉塞尔夫人之间，存在着一种可以称之为友谊的关系，尽管她们性格迥异——也许正是因为她们性格迥异，这种友谊才一直存在。

paragraphs.en: Marilla was a tall, thin woman, with angles and without curves; her dark hair showed some gray streaks and was always twisted up in a hard little knot behind with two wire hairpins stuck aggressively through it. She looked like a woman of narrow experience and rigid conscience, which she was; but there was a saving something about her mouth which, if it had been ever so slightly developed, might have been considered indicative of a sense of humor.
paragraphs.zh: 玛丽拉是个高挑瘦削的女人，浑身都是棱角，没有曲线；她漆黑的头发已有些灰白，总是紧紧地盘在脑后，用两根铁发夹强硬地插着。她看起来像个阅历狭窄、道德观念极强的女人，而她确实如此；但她的嘴边似乎有一种可贵的特质，若它稍加发展，或许会被认为是具有幽默感的征兆。

paragraphs.en: “We’re all pretty well,” said Mrs. Rachel. “I was kind of afraid _you_ weren’t, though, when I saw Matthew starting off today. I thought maybe he was going to the doctor’s.”
paragraphs.zh: “我们大家都挺好的，”拉塞尔太太说，“今天我看见马修出发的时候，我有点担心你是不是不太好，我还以为他要去医生那儿了。”

paragraphs.en: Marilla’s lips twitched understandingly. She had expected Mrs. Rachel up; she had known that the sight of Matthew jaunting off so unaccountably would be too much for her neighbor’s curiosity.
paragraphs.zh: 玛丽拉的嘴唇微微抽动，表示她明白。她本就料到拉塞尔太太会醒着，她知道马修如此莫名其妙地匆匆离去，对邻居的好奇心来说是难以忍受的。

paragraphs.en: “Oh, no, I’m quite well although I had a bad headache yesterday,” she said. “Matthew went to Bright River. We’re getting a little boy from an orphan asylum in Nova Scotia and he’s coming on the train tonight.”
paragraphs.zh: “哦，不，我很好，虽然昨天头痛了一天，”她说，“马修去了布莱特河。我们要从新斯科舍省的一个孤儿院领养一个男孩，他今晚坐火车过来。”

paragraphs.en: If Marilla had said that Matthew had gone to Bright River to meet a kangaroo from Australia Mrs. Rachel could not have been more astonished. She was actually stricken dumb for five seconds. It was unsupposable that Marilla was making fun of her, but Mrs. Rachel was almost forced to suppose it.
paragraphs.zh: 如果玛丽拉说马修去Bright River是去接一只来自澳大利亚的袋鼠，拉塞尔夫人不会有更惊讶的了。她真的愣住了五秒钟，说不出话来。虽然无法想象玛丽拉是在拿她开玩笑，但拉塞尔夫人几乎不得不这么认为。

paragraphs.en: “Are you in earnest, Marilla?” she demanded when voice returned to her.
paragraphs.zh: “你是在认真说吗，玛丽拉？”她声音恢复后质问道。

paragraphs.en: “Yes, of course,” said Marilla, as if getting boys from orphan asylums in Nova Scotia were part of the usual spring work on any well-regulated Avonlea farm instead of being an unheard of innovation.
paragraphs.zh: “是的，当然了，”玛丽拉说，仿佛从新斯科舍省的孤儿院领养男孩是任何正规的阿文利农场在春天的常规工作，而不是一种前所未有的新尝试。

paragraphs.en: Mrs. Rachel felt that she had received a severe mental jolt. She thought in exclamation points. A boy! Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert of all people adopting a boy! From an orphan asylum! Well, the world was certainly turning upside down! She would be surprised at nothing after this! Nothing!
paragraphs.zh: 拉塞尔夫人感到自己受到了严重的心理冲击。她用感叹号来思考。一个男孩！竟然是一向古板的玛丽拉和马修·卡思伯特收养了一个男孩！还是从孤儿院来的！天啊，世界真是彻底翻了个个儿！她对之后发生的一切都不会再感到惊讶了！什么都不奇怪了！

paragraphs.en: “What on earth put such a notion into your head?” she demanded disapprovingly.
paragraphs.zh: “你脑子里怎么会有这种想法？”她不满地质问道。

paragraphs.en: This had been done without her advice being asked, and must perforce be disapproved.
paragraphs.zh: 这并未征求她的意见，必须予以反对。

paragraphs.en: “Well, we’ve been thinking about it for some time--all winter in fact,” returned Marilla. “Mrs. Alexander Spencer was up here one day before Christmas and she said she was going to get a little girl from the asylum over in Hopeton in the spring. Her cousin lives there and Mrs. Spencer has visited her and knows all about it. So Matthew and I have talked it over off and on ever since. We thought we’d get a boy. Matthew is getting up in years, you know--he’s sixty--and he isn’t so spry as he once was. His heart troubles him a good deal. And you know how desperate hard it’s got to be to get hired help. There’s never anybody to be had but those stupid, half-grown little French boys; and as soon as you do get one broke into your ways and taught something he’s up and off to the lobster canneries or the States. At first Matthew suggested getting a Home boy. But I said ‘no’ flat to that. ‘They may be all right--I’m not saying they’re not--but no London street Arabs for me,’ I said. ‘Give me a native born at least. There’ll be a risk, no matter who we get. But I’ll feel easier in my mind and sleep sounder at nights if we get a born Canadian.’ So in the end we decided to ask Mrs. Spencer to pick us out one when she went over to get her little girl. We heard last week she was going, so we sent her word by Richard Spencer’s folks at Carmody to bring us a smart, likely boy of about ten or eleven. We decided that would be the best age--old enough to be of some use in doing chores right off and young enough to be trained up proper. We mean to give him a good home and schooling. We had a telegram from Mrs. Alexander Spencer today--the mail-man brought it from the station--saying they were coming on the five-thirty train tonight. So Matthew went to Bright River to meet him. Mrs. Spencer will drop him off there. Of course she goes on to White Sands station herself.”
paragraphs.zh: “嗯，我们已经考虑了一段时间了——实际上整个冬天都在考虑，”玛丽拉回答道。“圣诞节前有天亚历山大·斯宾塞太太来这里，她说她打算在春天从霍普顿的孤儿院领个女孩来。她的表亲住在那儿，斯宾塞太太去过那儿，对那儿的情况很了解。从那以后，马修和我就一直断断续续地讨论这件事。我们原本想领个男孩。你知道，马修年纪大了——他已经六十岁了——而且不像以前那么灵活了。他的心脏问题很严重。而且你明白，现在要找个佣人是多么困难。” 救命啊。要找个帮手简直不可能，只能找到那些愚蠢的、半大不小的法国男孩；可你刚把他教得有点模样，他就会跑掉，去罐头厂或者去美国了。起初马修建议找个本地男孩。但我坚决地说“不行”。“他们也许不错——我并不是说他们不好——但可别给我找伦敦街头的流浪儿，”我说，“至少要找个本地出生的。不管我们找谁，总归是有风险的。但要是找个加拿大本地出生的，我会觉得心里踏实些，晚上也能睡得安稳些。”所以最后我们决定请斯宾塞太太来…… 当她去接她的小女儿时，我们挑了一个。我们上周听说她要来，于是通过卡莫迪的理查德·斯宾塞家的人捎信，让我们带一个大约十到十一岁聪明、有出息的男孩来。我们认为这个年龄最合适——年纪大一点的话，可以马上帮忙做些杂活，年纪小一点的话，也容易好好培养。我们打算给他一个良好的家庭和教育。今天，我们收到了亚历山大·斯宾塞夫人的电报——邮差从车站带来的——说他们今晚乘五点半的火车过来。所以马修去布莱特河接他了。斯宾塞夫人 他会把她送到那里。当然，她自己会去怀特沙兹车站。

paragraphs.en: Mrs. Rachel prided herself on always speaking her mind; she proceeded to speak it now, having adjusted her mental attitude to this amazing piece of news.
paragraphs.zh: 雷切儿太太以总是直言不讳而自豪；她现在调整好了自己的心态，准备说出自己的想法，这则令人惊讶的消息让她如此。

paragraphs.en: “Well, Marilla, I’ll just tell you plain that I think you’re doing a mighty foolish thing--a risky thing, that’s what. You don’t know what you’re getting. You’re bringing a strange child into your house and home and you don’t know a single thing about him nor what his disposition is like nor what sort of parents he had nor how he’s likely to turn out. Why, it was only last week I read in the paper how a man and his wife up west of the Island took a boy out of an orphan asylum and he set fire to the house at night--set it _on purpose_, Marilla--and nearly burnt them to a crisp in their beds. And I know another case where an adopted boy used to suck the eggs--they couldn’t break him of it. If you had asked my advice in the matter--which you didn’t do, Marilla--I’d have said for mercy’s sake not to think of such a thing, that’s what.”
paragraphs.zh: “好吧，玛丽拉，我干脆直说了，我觉得你这么做非常愚蠢——真是个危险的举动。你根本不知道自己在搞什么。你把一个陌生的孩子带进你家，可你对他一无所知，不知道他的性格如何，不知道他父母是什么样的人，也不清楚他将来会变成什么样子。要知道，就在上周，我在报纸上看到，有个住在岛西边的男人和他妻子从孤儿院领养了一个男孩，结果这个男孩晚上放火烧了房子——是故意放的，玛丽拉——差点把他们烧死在床铺上。” 我知道另一个例子，有个被收养的男孩总是吃鸡蛋——他们怎么也改不了他这个习惯。如果你当时征求我的意见的话——你却没有征求，玛丽拉——我会说，看在上帝的份上，千万别打这种主意，就是这样。”

paragraphs.en: This Job’s comforting seemed neither to offend nor to alarm Marilla. She knitted steadily on.
paragraphs.zh: 这个工作让马莉拉感到安慰，这既没有冒犯她，也没有让她感到惊慌。她继续稳步地织着毛线。

paragraphs.en: “I don’t deny there’s something in what you say, Rachel. I’ve had some qualms myself. But Matthew was terrible set on it. I could see that, so I gave in. It’s so seldom Matthew sets his mind on anything that when he does I always feel it’s my duty to give in. And as for the risk, there’s risks in pretty near everything a body does in this world. There’s risks in people’s having children of their own if it comes to that--they don’t always turn out well. And then Nova Scotia is right close to the Island. It isn’t as if we were getting him from England or the States. He can’t be much different from ourselves.”
paragraphs.zh: “我并不否认你所说的有道理，瑞秋。我自己也有些犹豫。但马修却非常坚持。我能看出来，所以只好让步了。马修很少会坚持某件事，所以当他真的坚持的时候，我总觉得我有责任让步。至于风险，这世上几乎每件事都有风险。如果说到生孩子，那风险就更大了——他们并不总是能长大成才。而且新斯科舍离岛也很近，我们并不是从英格兰或美国把他接过来的，他应该不会有太大差别。” 从我们自己身上。

paragraphs.en: “Well, I hope it will turn out all right,” said Mrs. Rachel in a tone that plainly indicated her painful doubts. “Only don’t say I didn’t warn you if he burns Green Gables down or puts strychnine in the well--I heard of a case over in New Brunswick where an orphan asylum child did that and the whole family died in fearful agonies. Only, it was a girl in that instance.”
paragraphs.zh: “好吧，我希望一切都会好起来，”拉塞尔太太用一种明显表现出她痛苦疑虑的语气说道。“只是，如果他把绿屋烧了，或者在井里下毒——我听说过新不伦瑞克省有个孤儿院的孩子这么做过，结果全家人都在可怕的痛苦中死了。不过，那次是个女孩。”

paragraphs.en: “Well, we’re not getting a girl,” said Marilla, as if poisoning wells were a purely feminine accomplishment and not to be dreaded in the case of a boy. “I’d never dream of taking a girl to bring up. I wonder at Mrs. Alexander Spencer for doing it. But there, _she_ wouldn’t shrink from adopting a whole orphan asylum if she took it into her head.”
paragraphs.zh: “好吧，我们不会领养个女孩，”玛丽拉说，仿佛毒井是女性特有的本领，而男孩则不必担心。“我绝不会想到要领养个女孩来抚养。我真不明白亚历山大·斯宾塞太太怎么会这么做。不过，她要是打定主意的话，恐怕连整个孤儿院的孤儿都会收养。”

paragraphs.en: Mrs. Rachel would have liked to stay until Matthew came home with his imported orphan. But reflecting that it would be a good two hours at least before his arrival she concluded to go up the road to Robert Bell’s and tell the news. It would certainly make a sensation second to none, and Mrs. Rachel dearly loved to make a sensation. So she took herself away, somewhat to Marilla’s relief, for the latter felt her doubts and fears reviving under the influence of Mrs. Rachel’s pessimism.
paragraphs.zh: 拉塞尔夫人本来想等到马修带着他从国外带来的孤儿回来。但一想到马修至少还要两个小时才能到，她便决定沿着路去罗伯特·贝尔家，把这消息告诉他们。这消息肯定会引起极大的轰动，而拉塞尔夫人非常喜爱制造轰动。于是她离开了，这多少让玛丽拉感到松了一口气，因为玛丽拉在拉塞尔夫人悲观的言论影响下，自己的疑虑和恐惧又重新浮现出来。

paragraphs.en: “Well, of all things that ever were or will be!” ejaculated Mrs. Rachel when she was safely out in the lane. “It does really seem as if I must be dreaming. Well, I’m sorry for that poor young one and no mistake. Matthew and Marilla don’t know anything about children and they’ll expect him to be wiser and steadier than his own grandfather, if so be’s he ever had a grandfather, which is doubtful. It seems uncanny to think of a child at Green Gables somehow; there’s never been one there, for Matthew and Marilla were grown up when the new house was built--if they ever _were_ children, which is hard to believe when one looks at them. I wouldn’t be in that orphan’s shoes for anything. My, but I pity him, that’s what.”
paragraphs.zh: “天啊，世上竟然有这种事！”蕾切尔太太安全地走到小路上时感叹道。“这真像是我在做梦。好吧，我真为那个可怜的小家伙难过，一点没错。马修和玛丽拉根本不懂怎么照顾孩子，他们大概会指望这个孩子比他自己的爷爷还要聪明稳重，如果他真有爷爷的话，这还值得怀疑呢。想到有孩子在绿山墙农舍，真是有点怪怪的；那儿从来就没住过孩子，因为当新房子建好的时候，马修和玛丽拉已经长大了——如果他们曾经是孩子的话，这还很难说。 很难相信他们竟然会是这样。我宁愿做任何事，也不愿意成为那个孤儿。唉，我真同情他，真是可怜。

paragraphs.en: So said Mrs. Rachel to the wild rose bushes out of the fulness of her heart; but if she could have seen the child who was waiting patiently at the Bright River station at that very moment her pity would have been still deeper and more profound.
paragraphs.zh: Rachel太太真心实意地对那些野玫瑰丛说道；但如果她能看见此刻正耐心地在明亮河车站等待的那个孩子，她的怜悯之情将会更加深切和强烈。
